hints: Think about the formulae of the highest chlorides, $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{MgCl}_2$, $\text{AlCl}_3$, $\text{SiCl}_4$, $\text{PCl}_5$, and remember Cl is $\text{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Link chloride formula to oxidation number**
Chlorine in a chloride is always $\text{-1}$. So the oxidation number of the other element is just what is needed to balance the chlorides. $\text{NaCl}$ means Na must be $\text{+1}$, $\text{MgCl}_2$ means Mg must be $\text{+2}$, and so on up to $\text{PCl}_5$ where P must be $\text{+5}$.
Final answer: Na: +1, Mg: +2, Al: +3, Si: +4, P: +5

hints: Ask yourself what increases by one each step from Na to P that can be lost or shared to form bonds.
walkthrough:
See the pattern across the Period**
Moving from Na to P you add one outer electron each time. Na has 1, Mg has 2, up to P with 5. The maximum number you can use in bonding, by losing or sharing, sets the maximum oxidation number, so it matches the outer electron count.
Final answer: The number of outer shell / valence electrons.

hints: Recall that $\text{SiCl}_4$ is hydrolysed completely by water to give a solid oxide and a strong acid.
walkthrough:
Picture the hydrolysis**
$\text{SiCl}_4$ is a covalent tetrahedral chloride. Water attacks Si, Cl leaves as $\text{HCl}$. All four Cl atoms end up as $\text{HCl}$ and Si ends up as $\text{SiO}_2$. Balance O with 2 waters and H and Cl with 4 $\text{HCl}$: $\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2 + 4\text{HCl}$.

hints: Look at your products in (b)(i) and decide if $\text{HCl}$ makes the solution acidic, neutral or alkaline.
walkthrough:
Connect product to pH**
The reaction makes $\text{HCl}$, a strong acid that fully dissociates to give $\text{H}^+$. $\text{SiO}_2$ is insoluble and neutral. So the solution is strongly acidic, expect pH around 1 to 2.
Final answer: pH 1 to 4, strongly acidic due to $\text{HCl}$ formed.

hints: Remember P(V) chloride hydrolyses to phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, plus $\text{HCl}$.
walkthrough:
Build the products for P(V)**
With $\text{PCl}_5$, all five Cl atoms become $\text{HCl}$. Phosphorus ends up as phosphoric(V) acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. Count atoms: you need 4 $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply 8 H and 4 O, giving 5 $\text{HCl}$ plus $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. That balances: $\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 5\text{HCl} + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$.

hints: Both products, $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, are acids, so predict strongly acidic pH.
walkthrough:
Read acidity from products**
You are making a strong acid $\text{HCl}$ plus a weak acid $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. There is no base present, so the mixture must be strongly acidic with a low pH, typically 1 to 2.
Final answer: pH 1 to 4, strongly acidic due to $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$.

hints: Recall chlorine in water disproportionates to oxidation numbers 0 to +1 and -1, giving $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HOCl}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the disproportionation**
$\text{Cl}_2$ reacts reversibly with water. One Cl atom is oxidised to $\text{+1}$ in chloric(I) acid, $\text{HOCl}$, the other is reduced to $\text{-1}$ in $\text{HCl}$. Write it as an equilibrium: $\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HOCl} + \text{HCl}$.

hints: Remember hot concentrated alkali pushes chlorine to $\text{+5}$ in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ alongside $\text{Cl}^-$, not to $\text{ClO}^-$.
walkthrough:
Distinguish hot from cold**
Cold $\text{NaOH}$ gives $\text{NaClO}$ with Cl at $\text{+1}$. Hot $\text{NaOH}$ drives further disproportionation to chlorate(V), $\text{NaClO}_3$, with Cl at $\text{+5}$. Balance Cl, Na, O and H to get: $3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Think which ion comes from $\text{NaClO}$ when it dissolves, the $\text{Na}^+$ is spectator.
walkthrough:
Find the killing species**
$\text{NaClO}$ splits into $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{ClO}^-$. Sodium ions do nothing to bacteria. It is the chlorate(I) ion, $\text{ClO}^-$, that oxidises and kills bacteria.

hints: Use the names of the products, sodium chloride, water and oxygen, and balance atoms starting with Cl and O.
walkthrough:
Assemble the equation**
Reactants are $\text{NaClO}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$. Products are $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{O}_2$. Check atoms: Na 1 each side, Cl 1 each side, H 2 each side, O 3 each side. It is already balanced: $\text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Start from the gas volume, $42.0 \text{ cm}^3$, and convert to moles of $\text{O}_2$ using $24000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ at room conditions.
Use the 1:1 mole ratio from (e)(ii) to find moles of $\text{NaClO}$ in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ portion, then scale up to the full $100 \text{ cm}^3$ diluted solution.
Remember that $100 \text{ cm}^3$ diluted solution came from only $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ of W, so work out $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for W then multiply by $M_r$ of $\text{NaClO}$ ($74.5$).
walkthrough:
Convert gas to moles**
The gas is $\text{O}_2$ measured at room conditions, so molar volume is $24000 \text{ cm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$. $$n(\text{O}_2) = \frac{V}{24000} = \frac{42.0}{24000} = 1.75 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Scale through the dilution**
From (e)(ii), $1$ mol $\text{NaClO}$ gives $1$ mol $\text{O}_2$. So $25.0 \text{ cm}^3$ diluted bleach contained $1.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $\text{NaClO}$. The full $100 \text{ cm}^3$ flask holds 4 times this: $$n = 1.75 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{100}{25.0} = 7.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ This $7.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol came from the original $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ of W.

Convert to $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ of W**
First find molarity of W: $$c = \frac{7.00 \times 10^{-3}}{10.0/1000} = 0.700 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ $M_r(\text{NaClO}) = 23.0 + 35.5 + 16.0 = 74.5$. $$\text{concentration} = 0.700 \times 74.5 = 52.2 \text{ g dm}^{-3}$$

Final answer: mol $\text{O}_2$ = $42.0/24000 = 1.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol
mol $\text{NaClO}$ in $100 \text{ cm}^3$ diluted = $1.75 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 = 7.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol = mol in $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ W
concentration of W = $52.2 \text{ g dm}^{-3}$
